findings.title: Refund tool silently truncates a fractional subunit amount
findings.invariant: Money in currency subunits is an integer and invalid fractions must be rejected, never changed.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced against the official handler and SDK request path
findings.description: A generated black-box regression test invoked the official tool handler and intercepted its HTTP request.
findings.impact: An invalid fractional-subunit request reaches the API with a different value instead of failing closed. The mutation is less than one subunit, so this is an input-integrity defect rather than a large-value loss claim.
findings.counterexample: fractional money crossed the MCP boundary: requested=100.75 sent=100
findings.proposed_fix: Validate and store an int64 before invoking the SDK; upgrade the MCP dependency and publish an integer schema when supported.

findings.title: Checkout generator emits one-paise undercharge bugs across seven backend languages
findings.invariant: Major-to-minor currency conversion must be decimal-exact and produce the intended integer subunit value.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced; no matching public issue or pull request found
findings.description: Exact expressions emitted by the templates were executed on locally installed runtimes.
findings.impact: Fresh projects generated by Razorpay's official AI tool can create orders for less than the user-entered price. The defect is copied into merchant code, multiplying its blast radius.
findings.counterexample: ₹2.01 should be 201 paise; python, ruby, php returned 200. Node's rounded control returned 201.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the generated boundary accept integer subunits or exact decimal strings; reject excess precision and convert with a decimal type.

evidence.summary: Generated backend uses binary float then truncates

findings.title: Checkout generator applies a two-decimal multiplier to zero- and three-decimal currencies
findings.invariant: Major-to-minor conversion uses the exponent of the selected currency, not a hardcoded factor of 100.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced with the exact generated Node expression
findings.description: Executing the generator's currency-agnostic Math.round(amount * 100) produced a 100× JPY overcharge and roughly 10× KWD undercharge relative to Razorpay's documented subunits.
findings.impact: Generated merchants can charge JPY orders at 100 times the intended value and KWD/BHD/OMR orders at roughly one tenth of the intended value. The Test API accepts and persists both wrong integer amounts because they are valid provider inputs.
findings.proposed_fix: Accept integer currency subunits, or use an authoritative currency exponent table plus exact decimal parsing and the documented third-decimal-zero rule.

evidence.summary: Generated endpoint accepts arbitrary currency with a major-unit amount
Generated endpoint always applies the INR-style ×100 conversion
Razorpay documents integer subunits with JPY exponent 0 and KWD/BHD/OMR exponent 3
Hardcoded ×100 violates documented JPY and KWD exponent examples

findings.title: Checkout generator treats browser price and cart state as the merchant's authoritative order
findings.surface: generated order creation, verification, and checkout wiring
findings.invariant: A successful payment is bound server-side to one authoritative merchant quote containing amount, currency, and cart identity.
findings.originality: independently discovered; no matching public issue or pull request found
findings.description: The generated frontend sends amount from browser state, the backend creates an order directly from that amount/currency, and the verify route checks only the browser-returned Razorpay tuple. The wiring instructions preserve the cart in localStorage rather than creating an authoritative server quote.
findings.impact: A buyer can lower the browser-supplied amount, obtain and pay a valid low-value Razorpay order, and still receive a cryptographically valid success response that is not bound to the intended cart or price. Replaying a previously valid tuple is also not rejected by the generated verifier.
findings.counterexample: Tamper checkout total to 1.00, pay the resulting valid order, then present its valid order_id|payment_id signature beside the untouched high-value localStorage cart.
findings.proposed_fix: Create an immutable server-side quote from trusted SKU/pricing data, store its Razorpay order ID, and consume the paid tuple exactly once only after matching order, amount, currency, merchant, and fulfillment state.

evidence.summary: Generated browser sends the price to the order endpoint
Generated backend trusts browser amount and currency
Verifier authenticates only the submitted Razorpay tuple
Generator directs the agent to keep pending order state in browser storage
Razorpay says the server-created order ties the payment and secures the request from tampering

findings.title: Generated Node verifier turns malformed signature lengths into HTTP 500
findings.invariant: Untrusted malformed authentication input fails closed as a controlled client error.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced with the exact generated comparison operation
findings.description: The generated timingSafeEqual call throws Node's length exception for an untrusted one-byte signature, and the generated route catches it as HTTP 500.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller can create noisy server errors and false operational alarms on the public verify endpoint.
findings.proposed_fix: Strictly decode a 64-character lowercase/uppercase hexadecimal signature, reject invalid length/encoding with 400, then compare equal-length bytes.

evidence.summary: Generated verifier compares buffers without validating length or hex encoding
Catch block maps the thrown malformed-input path to HTTP 500
evidence.detail: res.status(500).json({ success: false, error: 'Payment verification failed' });

evidence.summary: Node throws on the generated unequal-length comparison

findings.title: Generated Android, iOS, Cordova, and native Capacitor success paths discard the payment signature
findings.invariant: A generated Orders API flow preserves order_id, payment_id, and razorpay_signature from Checkout through mandatory server verification.
findings.originality: independently discovered; no matching public issue or pull request found
findings.description: Android uses PaymentResultListener, which returns only payment_id, and sends an empty signature. iOS likewise chooses the no-data completion protocol and sends an empty signature. Cordova and native Capacitor use a legacy payment_id-only callback and omit the signature.
findings.impact: A customer can successfully pay, after which the generated backend must reject the success callback because a mandatory verification field is absent. The merchant sees a paid-but-failed checkout and risks duplicate fulfillment recovery, support incidents, or refund churn.
findings.counterexample: The generated Android and iOS request bodies contain razorpay_signature="" on every successful payment.
findings.proposed_fix: Use PaymentResultWithDataListener and RazorpayPaymentCompletionProtocolWithData, and use the official Cordova payment.success event/object so all three signed fields reach the backend.

evidence.summary: Generated Android verification request always sends an empty signature
Generated iOS verification request always sends an empty signature
Generated native Capacitor request omits razorpay_signature
Android PaymentResultListener returns only payment_id; WithData is required for order_id and signature
Official Cordova Orders flow uses payment.success data containing order ID and signature

findings.title: Mobile generator installs nonexistent or unrelated packages instead of Razorpay's official Cordova SDK
findings.surface: Cordova, Ionic, and Capacitor dependency instructions
findings.invariant: Generated payment integrations install a currently published dependency controlled by Razorpay's verified package identity.
findings.originality: independently discovered; no matching public issue or pull request found
findings.description: Cordova and Ionic emit a package name that is absent from npm. Capacitor instructs npm to install cordova-plugin-razorpay, currently an 'Empty package' maintained by a non-Razorpay account, while Razorpay's official package is com.razorpay.cordova.
findings.impact: Two generated integrations fail at installation. The Capacitor path crosses a package-identity boundary and can make developers install code from a third party under a payment-SDK-like name.
findings.counterexample: npm view com.nicholaswilliams.nicepay.razorpay returns E404; npm metadata identifies cordova-plugin-razorpay as an empty non-Razorpay package.
findings.proposed_fix: Emit only the official com.razorpay.cordova package and supported installation instructions, pin an intentional version range, and add registry owner/repository conformance checks in CI.

evidence.summary: Cordova and Ionic install a package absent from npm
Capacitor installs a similarly named non-Razorpay package
Razorpay's official Cordova package is com.razorpay.cordova
cordova-plugin-razorpay is described as an empty package and is not maintained by Razorpay

findings.title: Repeated expand[] values collapse to the last value
findings.invariant: Repeated query parameters preserve multiplicity and order.
findings.originality: publicly reported and source-confirmed; the linked pull request is not maintainer acceptance
findings.description: The loop overwrites one map key for every requested expansion.
findings.impact: Callers asking for multiple expansions receive only the final expansion.
findings.proposed_fix: Represent repeated query values as a list and encode every occurrence.

findings.title: Refund tool omits header idempotency and hides receipt safety semantics
findings.invariant: A retryable money-moving action exposes and preserves effect identity.
findings.originality: publicly reported safety gap; the linked pull request is not maintainer acceptance
findings.description: The tool cannot send X-Refund-Idempotency and describes receipt only as an internal reference, even though Razorpay documents a stable receipt as an idempotency key.
findings.impact: A caller that omits receipt can create another refund on retry by design. A caller that reuses a stable receipt already has duplicate protection, so this is a safety/discoverability gap rather than a broken refund API.
findings.counterexample: No identity is intentionally a new refund; stable receipt or X-Refund-Idempotency identifies one effect.
findings.proposed_fix: Document receipt as the existing idempotency mechanism and also expose X-Refund-Idempotency for explicit retry identity.

evidence.summary: Tool exposes receipt but describes it only as internal reference
Refund SDK call passes nil headers

findings.title: .NET onboarding signatures reuse an AES-GCM nonce derived from the secret key
findings.invariant: AES-GCM uses a fresh unique nonce for every encryption under a key.
findings.originality: independently discovered and executed against the official SDK
findings.description: Two official SDK calls with identical input and key returned identical ciphertext.
findings.impact: Nonce reuse breaks AES-GCM confidentiality and authentication guarantees; repeated onboarding signatures become deterministic and related plaintexts leak keystream relations.
findings.counterexample: {"client_a_signature_accepted_after_b": false, "client_a_signature_error": "SignatureVerificationError: Invalid signature passed", "client_b_inherited_a_header": true, "first_prefix": "19607e8e4c0d48fb606b168a", "gcm_same": true, "key_after_b": "merchant_B", "key_before_b": "merchant_A", "unicode_accepted": false, "unicode_error": "SignatureVerificationError: Invalid signature passed"}
findings.proposed_fix: Generate 12 random bytes per call and return nonce || ciphertext || 16-byte tag, matching the other current SDKs.

evidence.summary: IV is deterministically copied from the key
Ruby release documents the same nonce-reuse defect and fixed wire format

findings.title: .NET signature verification uses ordinary string equality
findings.invariant: Authentication tags are compared in constant time.
findings.originality: publicly proposed hardening and independently source-confirmed; no practical remote exploit reproduced
findings.description: The verifier uses String.Equals rather than a fixed-time byte comparison.
findings.impact: Ordinary equality is functionally correct. A fixed-time comparison reduces timing leakage, but practical remote exploitability was not reproduced or claimed.
findings.proposed_fix: Decode hex and call CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals.

evidence.summary: Non-constant-time comparison

findings.title: Ruby payment-link verification depends on Hash insertion order
findings.invariant: The signed field order is protocol-defined, not caller-container-defined.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced; no matching public report found
findings.description: The official SDK accepted a correctly signed docs-order Hash and rejected the identical key/value set inserted in another order.
findings.impact: An authentic callback fails verification when the application builds the same field set in a different order; extra fields also contaminate the signature payload.
findings.proposed_fix: Read the four named fields explicitly in the protocol-defined order and do not mutate the caller's Hash.

evidence.summary: Signature payload follows Hash insertion order
Same signed fields: ordered accepted, reordered rejected

findings.title: Python webhook verifier rejects the raw bytes the webhook contract asks callers to preserve

findings.originality: publicly reported compatibility issue, independently reproduced against the pinned official commit
findings.description: A valid HMAC over a bytes payload throws before comparison.
findings.impact: Framework integrations that correctly retain the raw body cannot pass it to the SDK.
findings.counterexample: TypeError: encoding without a string argument
findings.proposed_fix: Encode str inputs and preserve bytes/bytearray inputs.

findings.title: Node webhook verifier uses ordinary string equality
findings.invariant: Authentication tags are compared in constant time.
findings.originality: publicly reported hardening concern; no maintainer confirmation or practical exploit reproduction
findings.description: The SDK compares hex HMACs with JavaScript strict equality.
findings.impact: Strict equality is functionally correct. A timing-safe comparison is defensive hardening; practical remote exploitability was not reproduced or claimed.
findings.proposed_fix: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual after strict length and hex validation.

findings.title: Java webhook HMAC payload uses the process default charset
findings.invariant: String compatibility APIs encode exact UTF-8 deterministically.
findings.originality: publicly reported compatibility issue and independently source-confirmed; not maintainer-confirmed
findings.description: The secret is explicitly UTF-8 but the payload calls getBytes() with no charset.
findings.impact: Unicode verification can depend on host locale on Java versions/configurations with a non-UTF-8 default. Java 18+ defaults to UTF-8, so this is conditional rather than universal.
findings.proposed_fix: Use StandardCharsets.UTF_8 and add a byte[] verifier.

evidence.summary: Default-charset payload encoding

findings.title: .NET client instances overwrite one process-wide credential and routing context
findings.surface: RazorpayClient, RestClient, and payment signature verification
findings.invariant: Credentials, base URL, access token, and request headers are scoped to one client instance and cannot be changed by constructing another client.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced against the pinned official SDK
findings.description: The official SDK probe initialized client A, added A's partner header, then initialized B. The global key changed to B, B inherited A's header, and A's valid payment signature failed because verification used B's secret.
findings.impact: A multi-tenant or multi-account .NET process can authenticate client A's request as client B, route it with another account's X-Razorpay-Account header, or reject A's valid payment signature after B is initialized.
findings.counterexample: {"client_a_signature_accepted_after_b": false, "client_a_signature_error": "SignatureVerificationError: Invalid signature passed", "client_b_inherited_a_header": true, "first_prefix": "19607e8e4c0d48fb606b168a", "gcm_same": true, "key_after_b": "merchant_B", "key_before_b": "merchant_A", "unicode_accepted": false, "unicode_error": "SignatureVerificationError: Invalid signature passed"}
findings.proposed_fix: Make all authentication, endpoint, header, and utility state immutable instance fields; bind resource clients and verification calls to an explicit client or secret.

evidence.summary: API key is process-global
API secret is process-global
Partner routing and custom headers are process-global
Every request reads current global credentials
Payment verification reads the current global secret
Two-client official .NET SDK probe crossed credential, header, and verifier state

findings.title: PHP client instances share and overwrite process-wide credentials and headers
findings.invariant: Each SDK client owns immutable credentials, base URL, token, and headers for its requests.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced against the pinned official SDK
findings.description: Constructing client B replaced the key visible to client A's process, while client B inherited the partner-routing header set through client A.
findings.impact: Long-running PHP workers serving multiple merchants can send one merchant's operation under another merchant's credentials or partner routing header, crossing account and tenant boundaries.
findings.proposed_fix: Move authentication, base URL, app details, and headers to instance-owned request clients, and inject that request client into every resource.

evidence.summary: API key is process-global
Each constructor overwrites the process-global key
Resources are created without an owning client context
Requests resolve the latest global credentials at call time
Request headers are process-global
Two official Api instances demonstrably share credentials and partner headers

findings.title: Java clients share one process-wide partner-routing header map
findings.invariant: X-Razorpay-Account and custom headers are scoped to the intended client or request.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced against the pinned official SDK
findings.description: Client B inherited client A's X-Razorpay-Account before B set any header; B then overwrote the single map for the whole process.
findings.impact: In an aggregator process, setting X-Razorpay-Account for one sub-merchant can silently route later requests from every other client to that same sub-merchant.
findings.proposed_fix: Store immutable default headers per RazorpayClient/resource and support per-request overrides; never use a mutable static routing map.

evidence.summary: All Java client instances share one header map
Instance method writes the global header map
Every request reads the global header map
Razorpay uses X-Razorpay-Account to select the sub-merchant for partner API calls

findings.title: Java document uploads mislabel runtime JPG and PNG paths as PDF
findings.invariant: Multipart file MIME type matches the selected file format.
findings.originality: independently discovered and reproduced against the pinned official SDK
